item.title: AI Coding Agent Risks, Entra Passkey Vishing, and Ubiquiti UniFi CVE-2026-50746
item.content:encoded:
Ubiquiti Patches Critical UniFi Flaws Across Connect, Talk, Access, Protect, and OS — Must Read

Ubiquiti released patches for multiple critical flaws in UniFi Connect, Talk, Access, Protect, and OS that could allow network-accessible attackers to escalate privileges or execute commands. Users should update to the fixed versions immediately, though there is no evidence these specific flaws have been exploited in the wild.

  • Ubiquiti shipped updates to address multiple critical security flaws affecting UniFi Connect, UniFi Talk, UniFi Access, UniFi Protect, and UniFi OS.
  • The vulnerabilities could allow attackers with network access to escalate privileges or execute arbitrary commands on host devices.
  • The highest-rated flaw is CVE-2026-50746, a CVSS 10.0 improper access control issue in the UniFi Connect Application fixed in version 3.4.20.
  • Other listed flaws include SQL injection in UniFi Talk, command injection and improper access control in UniFi Access, SSRF in UniFi Protect, and command injection and improper access control in UniFi OS.
  • The article states there is no evidence these flaws have been exploited in the wild, but notes that other UniFi OS vulnerabilities were flagged by CISA as weaponized last month.

Entra passkey enrollment vishing targets Microsoft 365 users — Should Read

A threat actor linked to the Pink extortion group is vishing Microsoft 365 users by pretending they must enroll a new Microsoft Entra passkey, then using a fake enrollment portal to capture credentials and register attacker-controlled passkeys. Successful compromises are used to quickly steal data from services like SharePoint and OneDrive.

  • A threat actor has been calling Microsoft 365 users and trying to convince them to enroll a new Microsoft Entra passkey controlled by the attacker.
  • Okta attributes the campaign to O-UNC-066, an actor operating the Pink extortion operation, which has targeted organizations in the food and beverage, technology, healthcare, automotive, construction, and aviation industries.
  • The phishing sites use victim organization branding and imitate the real Microsoft Entra passkey enrollment portal while guiding victims through authentication in near real time.
  • The phishing kit can adapt the victim experience based on the multi-factor authentication method used, including TOTP, push notifications with number matching, and SMS one-time passwords.
  • After gaining access to a victim's account, Pink quickly exfiltrates data from SharePoint and OneDrive services, according to researchers.

Taiwan charges two businessmen over alleged role in Chinese espionage campaign — Should Read

Taiwan charged two local businessmen with helping Chinese government-linked hackers rent LINE accounts used to impersonate journalists and target politicians, academics, journalists and civil society figures with phishing and malware. The case supports earlier research tying the campaign to a broader Beijing-linked espionage operation.

  • Taiwanese authorities charged two local businessmen with helping Chinese government-linked hackers conduct an espionage campaign targeting politicians, academics, journalists, and civil society groups.
  • Taiwan's Ministry of Justice Investigation Bureau said the suspects ran a company that collected and leased LINE accounts to operators linked to China's cyber forces.
  • Authorities allege the leased LINE accounts were used to impersonate international journalists, including reporters affiliated with the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists, to build trust with targets and deploy malware.
  • Investigators said the operation used malware disguised as encrypted communications software, with attackers encouraging victims to download the fake software.
  • The case provides official support for findings by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists and The Citizen Lab about a broad Beijing-linked phishing campaign targeting journalists, democracy activists, and members of Uyghur, Tibetan, Hong Kong, and Taiwanese communities abroad.

New HalluSquatting Attack Could Trick AI Coding Assistants Into Installing Botnet Malware — Should Read

Researchers describe HalluSquatting, an attack where adversaries register names that AI coding assistants predictably hallucinate for popular repositories or plugins, then use hidden prompt-injection instructions to make the assistant fetch and run attacker code. The key defense is to prevent agents from automatically installing or executing fetched resources without verifying the real source.

  • Researchers call the new attack HalluSquatting, where attackers identify fake resource names that AI coding assistants reliably invent, register those names, and wait for assistants to fetch the attacker-controlled resource.
  • The attack combines AI hallucinations with indirect prompt injection, using hidden instructions in a fetched repository or plugin to hijack an assistant that has permission to run commands.
  • In experiments, assistants reached for the same wrong name in up to 85% of repository requests and 100% of skill installs, and tools including Cursor, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, Cline, Gemini CLI, and OpenClaw were made to run harmless attacker-supplied code.
  • The researchers frame the technique as a way to assemble a botnet because one planted fake name tied to a popular resource could reach many machines across different operating systems.
  • The article says the most effective mitigation is for assistants to search before fetching resources, while users should avoid unattended auto-run modes and verify repository or package names before letting an agent pull them in.

AI Coding Agents Found Triggering Endpoint Security Rules Built to Catch Attackers — Should Read

Sophos found that AI coding agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and OpenAI Codex are triggering endpoint security rules because their normal tasks can resemble attacker behavior, including credential access, LOLBin downloads, and persistence changes. Defenders may need to tune noisy execution alerts around known agents, but should continue blocking agent access to credential stores and other high-risk actions.

  • Sophos analyzed seven days of June 2026 Windows endpoint telemetry and found AI coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, and OpenAI Codex triggering behavioral detection rules built to catch intruders.
  • Sophos said credential access accounted for 56.2 percent of the blocked activity, while execution accounted for 28.8 percent.
  • Claude Code activity included DPAPI-based browser credential decryption through GStack’s /browse skill and use of cmdkey /list to enumerate Windows Credential Manager entries, with one case involving the --dangerously-skip-permissions mode.
  • OpenAI Codex attempted to fetch a Python installer from python.org using certutil, then switched to bitsadmin after the first method was blocked.
  • Sophos recommended scoping some execution-related noise around known agent processes and paths, but said credential-store access should remain restricted even when performed by an AI agent.

Former UK privacy chief preparing legal action against woman who reported him, minister says — May Read

UK Science Secretary Liz Kendall said she was appalled by an independent investigation that upheld sexual harassment and bullying allegations against former Information Commissioner John Edwards, who resigned in June. She also told Parliament that Edwards is preparing legal action against one of the women who reported concerns, prompting a new review of the ICO’s culture, accountability and governance.

  • Liz Kendall told the Science, Innovation and Technology Committee that she was “absolutely appalled” by independent investigation findings of sexual harassment and bullying at the Information Commissioner’s Office.
  • Kendall said former Information Commissioner John Edwards is preparing to serve legal papers on one of the women at the ICO who raised concerns about his behavior earlier this year.
  • John Edwards formally resigned in June after voluntarily stepping back from his duties in February amid a workplace investigation into unspecified conduct.
  • Edwards wrote on LinkedIn that he had exercised poor judgment and made attempts at humor that were inappropriate and caused offense, though he said he did not agree with how the investigation was conducted.
  • Kendall said the government will launch an independent review of the ICO’s culture, accountability and governance, begin recruiting Edwards’ successor, and appoint a new board of non-executive directors, the majority of whom will be women.

Building a Mental Model for Kubernetes Security Research — Optional

The article presents a Kubernetes and AKS security research framework that organizes cluster behavior around control, identity, authorization, admission, workloads, data, compute, networking, and observability. Its main takeaway is that turning this mental model into YAML-driven cluster and workload scenarios makes Kubernetes security posture easier to study, compare, and eventually assess in real production environments.

  • The article argues that Kubernetes security analysis is difficult in production because clusters and their surrounding identity, access, configuration, and application-behavior information change quickly and grow in volume.
  • The author describes a mental model for AKS security research organized around lenses such as cluster control, credential retrieval, authentication, authorization, admission, workload management, data and storage, computing, networking, and observability.
  • The framework turns that mental model into a YAML-based cluster specification that Terraform uses to deploy AKS scenarios with deliberate choices such as managed Entra authentication, Azure RBAC for Kubernetes authorization, and workload identity.
  • The workload side of the framework includes FastAPI applications that can exercise multiple Azure authentication mechanisms, including client secret, certificate, managed identity, and federated workload identity.
  • The author’s longer-term goal is to use the framework’s controlled scenarios to build tools and tradecraft for collecting and analyzing real Kubernetes environments whose configurations and trust paths continue to change over time.

What the Black Hat NOC Taught Me About MCP & Agentic SOCs (Chapter 2 of 4) | Corelight — Optional

Corelight argues that the Black Hat NOC showed how AI agents and MCP can help SOC teams work faster, but only when they are grounded in high-quality network telemetry, constrained tools, and human oversight.

  • The article is titled “What the Black Hat NOC Taught Me About MCP & Agentic SOCs.”
  • The article is published by Corelight.
  • The article is presented as Chapter 2 of a four-part series.
  • The article focuses on lessons from the Black Hat NOC related to MCP and agentic SOCs.

3 Ways AI Powers Service Desk Attacks and How to Prevent Them — Optional

AI is making service desk social engineering more convincing and scalable, especially during employee onboarding when identities are less familiar. Organizations should reduce reliance on agent judgment by using stronger identity verification and secure credential setup before resets or access changes.

  • IBM’s 2025 Cost of a Data Breach Report found that 16% of studied breaches involved attackers using AI tools, most often for phishing or deepfake impersonation attacks.
  • The article says service desks are a natural target for social engineering because attackers who convince an agent they are legitimate may be able to get help bypassing technical controls.
  • AI can help attackers create polished emails, convincing chat messages, realistic call scripts, and AI-generated voice or video to impersonate employees.
  • Onboarding is described as especially exposed because new employees need fast access and service desk teams may not yet be familiar with who they are.
  • The article recommends securing onboarding with stronger identity verification, biometric liveness detection, and secure enrollment links that let new hires create their own passwords instead of receiving credentials by SMS or email.
